paragraphs: Wayve’s simulation team’s mission is to accelerate AV2.0 by incubating capabilities that become company‑level advantages, with generative world models and the synthetic data they produce as a key focus. You sit between ML research and engineering, collaborating with scientists on architecture and conditioning while working with platform engineers on generation jobs, training artefacts and the mixing of synthetic data into training. The role also demands strong Python and PyTorch (or equivalent) together with comfort in GPU training, debugging and reading model code.

I meet the Python requirement through multiple projects. Using scikit‑learn, TensorFlow and Keras I built end‑to‑end models that were served via FastAPI within Docker containers, demonstrating research engineering and collaboration with data scientists. In another effort I constructed a Python‑based data pipeline deployed with Docker and AWS Lambda, managing IAM permissions and processing numerous source datasets, which reinforced my ability to deliver reliable code at scale. These implementations were reviewed jointly with senior engineers, ensuring that the code adhered to best practices and facilitated smooth hand‑over to production teams.

The PyTorch requirement is satisfied by my work on GPU‑accelerated training pipelines. I developed a deep learning model in PyTorch that leveraged CUDA within Dockerised environments to ensure reproducible builds and efficient GPU utilisation. This setup allowed me to iterate rapidly on model architectures, debug low‑level performance issues and integrate the resulting checkpoints into downstream training workflows, confirming that the generated artefacts meet the quality standards expected for autonomous‑driving research. By containerising the PyTorch workflow I also enabled other researchers to launch generation jobs on shared GPU clusters, supporting collaborative experiments and rapid evaluation of synthetic data impact.
